entries.name: Qasim Amin
entries.desc: Qasim Amin was an Egyptian jurist and Islamic modernist, a co-founder of Cairo University and often counted among the Arab world's first feminists. Born in Alexandria, he took a law degree in Egypt and studied at Montpellier in France, and from 1885 served in Egypt's courts. He criticised veiling, seclusion, early marriage and the lack of education for women, and his book The Liberation of Women, published in 1899, called for an end to the veil. His advocacy stirred debate across the Arab world, though scholars such as Leila Ahmed have questioned his feminism.

entries.name: Jurji Zaydan
entries.desc: Jurji Zaydan was a Lebanese novelist, journalist and teacher of the Nahda who settled in Cairo and founded the magazine al-Hilal there in 1892. Born in Beirut to an Orthodox Christian family, he studied medicine at the Syrian Protestant College before moving to Egypt. His historical novels, about one a year from 1891 and serialised in al-Hilal, aimed to teach ordinary Arabs their own history. His secular History of Islamic Civilisation, published from 1901 to 1906, was controversial, and in 1910 public objections cost him a chair at the new Egyptian University.

entries.name: Prince Gong
entries.desc: Yixin, Prince Gong, was a Qing imperial prince and statesman, the sixth son of the Daoguang Emperor and a leader of China's Self-Strengthening Movement. Left behind with full powers when the Xianfeng Emperor fled Beijing in 1860, he signed the Convention of Peking with the British, French and Russians. In 1861 he set up the Zongli Yamen, in effect a foreign ministry, and joined the Empresses Dowager Ci'an and Cixi in a coup against the late emperor's regents, serving as prince-regent until 1865. Cixi dismissed him in 1884 and recalled him in 1894.

entries.name: Wenxiang
entries.desc: Wenxiang was a Manchu statesman of China's Qing dynasty, a bannerman of the Plain Red Banner, and one of the architects of the Self-Strengthening Movement. After gaining the jinshi, the highest degree of the imperial examination, in 1845, he joined the Grand Council in 1858. When the Xianfeng Emperor fled Beijing during the Second Opium War, he stayed and took part in the negotiations with the British and French. A founder of the Zongli Yamen, he was instrumental in devising the government's policy of cooperation with the Western powers between 1861 and 1876.

entries.name: Zhang Zhidong
entries.desc: Zhang Zhidong was a Chinese official of the late Qing dynasty who advocated controlled reform and the modernisation of the army, serving as viceroy of Huguang from 1889. He ordered an iron and steel plant from England, which began production in 1894 but made substantial losses, and founded a mint, mills and factories. His Exhortation to Study of 1898 summed up his relatively conservative reform in the phrase "Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for application". He took a leading role in abolishing the imperial examination in 1905.

entries.name: Yung Wing
entries.desc: Yung Wing was a Chinese-American diplomat and businessman who in 1854 became the first recorded Chinese graduate of an American university, Yale College. In 1863 Zeng Guofan sent him to the United States to buy machinery, which went into the Jiangnan Arsenal at Shanghai. He persuaded the Qing government to send young students abroad and organised the Chinese Educational Mission, which brought 120 of them to New England from 1872 until it was disbanded in 1881. A naturalised American citizen from 1852, he lost that status under the Chinese Exclusion Act.

entries.name: Zongli Yamen
entries.desc: The Zongli Yamen was the office in charge of foreign policy in China under the late Qing dynasty, set up by Prince Gong in 1861 after the Convention of Peking. Before it, foreign relations had been handled by several agencies, among them the Ministry of Rites and the Lifan Yuan. It was supervised by five senior officials, at first all Manchus, with Prince Gong as their leader in practice, and from 1875 it opened legations and consulates abroad. The Boxer Protocol of 1901 replaced it with a Foreign Office, the Waiwubu.

entries.name: Tongwen Guan
entries.desc: The Tongwen Guan, or School of Combined Learning, was a government school of Western languages and science founded at Beijing in 1862 to train interpreters for the Zongli Yamen. It opened with ten students of English; a proposal to add astronomy and mathematics was opposed by conservatives led by Woren, who feared "learning from foreigners". By 1877, with W. A. P. Martin as dean, it taught foreign languages and subjects from chemistry to international law to over a hundred students. In 1902 it was absorbed into the Imperial University of Peking, now Peking University.

entries.name: Jiangnan Arsenal
entries.desc: The Jiangnan Arsenal was a state-owned arms factory and shipyard at Shanghai, planned under Zeng Guofan and set up by Li Hongzhang in 1865 during the Self-Strengthening Movement. It combined a plant bought from an American firm, the assets of the Suzhou and Anqing arsenals and machinery Yung Wing bought in the United States. The largest of the movement's arsenals, it built its first steamship, the Huiji, in 1868 and ran a language school and a translation house. Its shipyard, split off in 1905, survives as the Jiangnan Shipyard; its arms works closed in 1937.

entries.name: Fuzhou Navy Yard
entries.desc: The Fuzhou Navy Yard, or Foochow Arsenal, was a shipyard at Mawei in Fuzhou prefecture, created by the Qing Empire with French help during the Self-Strengthening Movement. Planned from 1866 under Zuo Zongtang with a naval college, it was built from 1867 under the French naval officers Prosper Giquel and Paul d'Aiguebelle, contracted to provide within five years a dockyard, eleven transports, five gunboats and schools of navigation and marine engineering. Its first ship, the Wannian Qing, was launched in June 1869. French forces severely damaged the yard during the Sino-French War in 1884.

entries.name: Beiyang Fleet
entries.desc: The Beiyang Fleet, or Northern Ocean Fleet, was one of four regional navies of late Qing China, sponsored by Li Hongzhang to guard the approaches to Beijing. Begun in 1871 and equipped mostly with warships built in Germany and Britain, among them the battleships Dingyuan and Zhenyuan, it was the largest fleet in Asia in the late 1880s. In 1888 it was formally placed under the Navy Yamen, and its budget was cut. Under Ding Ruchang it suffered heavy losses at the Battle of the Yalu River in 1894 and was annihilated at Weihaiwei.

entries.name: Robert Hart
entries.desc: Sir Robert Hart was a British official serving Qing China, the second inspector-general of its Imperial Maritime Customs Service, which he headed for over four decades from 1863. Born in Portadown, Ireland, he came to China in 1854 as a student interpreter and joined the customs at Canton in 1859. Responsible for collecting customs duties for the Chinese government, he extended the service to more ports, standardised its work and insisted on efficiency and honesty; a modern postal service was later added. In 1862 he helped Prince Gong set up the Tongwen Guan.
